hook_text: Fire, flood, earthquake, violence. Four ways to lose a home in one night, and one question: where does the family sleep?
clip_script: Two in the morning in Khayelitsha. A stove tips, the wind catches it, and shacks a metre apart go one after another. By dawn, ash and iron sheets and people in what they were wearing. April 2022, KwaZulu-Natal: 300 millimetres of rain in a day, rivers through the settlements, homes washed off slopes, four hundred dead, roads gone, mud everywhere. Orkney, 2014: the ground shakes, walls crack, and nobody can go back inside until an engineer says so. 2008: violence empties streets and fills police stations with families who cannot go home. Four disasters, one brief: a shelter within hours, for a family, sturdy, waterproof, floored, up in an hour by the people themselves, light, lasting a month, safe from the stove that will be used inside. And technology on both sides: the stove and the blocked drain that caused it, the tent and the phone alert that answer it.
visual_style: Whiteboard four panels: flame between shacks, rising water line, cracked wall, emptied street; a shared brief list appearing under all four; stove and tent icons facing each other.
mood: Sober and purposeful, moving from loss to design.
pacing: Fire, flood, quake, strife, brief, technology, each a few seconds.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and write what a shelter must do in each of the four scenarios.
